Isa Whitney, brother of the late Elias Whitney, D.D., Principal of the Theological College of St. George’s, was deeply addicted to opium. As I understand it, the habit began with a foolish experiment during his college days. After reading De Quincey’s account of his dreams and sensations, he soaked his tobacco in laudanum, hoping to produce the same effects. He discovered, as so many others have, that the practice is easier to acquire than to abandon. For years he remained a slave to the drug, inspiring both horror and pity in his friends and relations. I can picture him still: his yellow, pasty face, his drooping eyelids and pin-point pupils, his body huddled in a chair—the ruined remains of a noble man.

One night in June 1889, our doorbell rang at about the hour when a man begins to yawn and look at the clock. I straightened up in my chair. My wife lowered her needlework into her lap, with a little expression of disappointment.
“A patient!” she said. “You will have to go out.”
I groaned; I had only just returned after an exhausting day.
We heard the front door open, a few hurried words, then quick footsteps on the linoleum. The door of our room flew open, and a woman in a dark dress and black veil came in.

“Please forgive me for calling so late,” she began. Then, suddenly losing command of herself, she hurried forward, put her arms around my wife’s neck, and sobbed on her shoulder. “Oh, I’m in such trouble!” she cried. “I need a little help so badly.”
“Why, it is Kate Whitney!” my wife said, lifting her veil. “How you startled me, Kate! When you came in, I had no idea who you were.”
“I did not know what to do, so I came directly to you.” It was always like that. People in distress came to my wife as birds come to a lighthouse.
“It was very kind of you to come. Now have some wine and water, sit comfortably here, and tell us everything. Or would you prefer me to send James off to bed?”
“Oh, no, no! I need the doctor’s advice and help as well. It is about Isa. He has not come home for two days. I am so afraid for him!”

She had spoken to us before about her husband’s troubles—to me as a doctor, and to my wife as an old friend from school. We did our best to soothe and comfort her. Did she know where he was? Could we perhaps bring him home to her?

Apparently we could. She had reliable information that lately, when the craving seized him, he had been visiting an opium den at the far eastern end of the City. Until now, these bouts had lasted only a day, and he had returned in the evening, twitching and exhausted. This time, however, the spell had held him for forty-eight hours. No doubt he was lying there among the dregs of the docks, inhaling the poison or sleeping off its effects. She was certain we would find him at the Bar of Gold in Upper Swandam Lane. But what could she do? How could a young, timid woman enter such a place and drag her husband away from the ruffians surrounding him?

That was the situation, and naturally there was only one answer. Could I not accompany her there? Then another thought occurred to me: why should she go at all? As Isa Whitney’s medical adviser, I had some influence over him and could manage better alone. I gave her my word that, if he really was at the address she had supplied, I would send him home in a cab within two hours. Ten minutes later I had left my armchair and cheerful sitting-room behind and was travelling east in a hansom. It seemed a strange errand at the time, though only what followed could reveal how strange it would become.

The first stage of my adventure, however, presented little difficulty. Upper Swandam Lane is a filthy alley hidden behind the high wharves on the north bank of the river, east of London Bridge. Between a cheap clothing shop and a gin-shop, a steep staircase descended to a dark opening like the mouth of a cave. There I found the den I wanted. I told the cabman to wait and went down the steps, their centres worn hollow by the endless tread of drunken feet. By a flickering oil lamp above the door, I located the latch and entered a long, low room. Brown opium smoke hung thick and heavy in it, and rows of wooden sleeping berths rose in tiers like those in the forecastle of an emigrant ship.

In the gloom I could just make out bodies sprawled in bizarre positions: hunched shoulders, drawn-up knees, heads tilted back, chins pointing upwards. Here and there a dark, dull eye turned towards the newcomer. Small red circles glimmered from the black shadows, brightening and fading as the poisonous substance burned in the bowls of metal pipes. Most of the occupants were silent. Some muttered to themselves; others conversed in strange, low, monotonous tones, their talk spilling out in bursts before suddenly falling silent. Each mumbled his own thoughts with little attention to his neighbour’s words. At the far end stood a small brazier of burning charcoal. Beside it, on a three-legged wooden stool, sat a tall, thin old man, his jaw resting on his two fists and his elbows on his knees, staring into the fire.
As I came in, a sallow Malay attendant hurried towards me with a pipe and a supply of opium, gesturing towards an empty berth.
“Thank you, but I do not intend to stay,” I said. “A friend of mine is here, Mr. Isa Whitney, and I want to speak to him.”
Someone moved and exclaimed on my right. Peering into the darkness, I saw Whitney staring at me, pale, haggard, and dishevelled.
“My God! It’s Watson,” he said. He was suffering a miserable reaction to the drug, every nerve trembling. “Tell me, Watson, what time is it?”
“Almost eleven.”
“On what day?”
“Friday, the nineteenth of June.”
“Good heavens! I thought it was Wednesday. It is Wednesday. Why do you want to frighten a fellow?” He buried his face in his arms and began sobbing in a high-pitched voice.
“I assure you it is Friday. Your wife has been waiting two days for you. You ought to be ashamed of yourself!”

“I am. But you are mistaken, Watson. I have only been here a few hours—three pipes, four pipes, I cannot remember how many. Still, I will come home with you. I would not frighten Kate, poor little Kate. Give me your hand! Have you brought a cab?”
“Yes, there is one waiting outside.”
“Then I will take it. But I must owe them something. Find out how much, Watson. I feel terribly unwell. I cannot do anything for myself.”

I walked along the narrow aisle between the two rows of sleepers, holding my breath against the drug’s foul, stupefying fumes and looking for the manager. As I passed the tall man beside the brazier, I felt a sudden tug at the skirt of my coat. A quiet voice whispered, “Walk past me, then look back.” I heard the words distinctly. I glanced down. They could only have come from the old man beside me, yet he sat apparently as absorbed as before: thin, deeply wrinkled, and stooping with age. An opium pipe hung between his knees, as though exhaustion had made him let it slip from his fingers. I took two steps and turned. Only the greatest effort kept me from crying out in astonishment. He had turned his back on the room so that only I could see him. His body had filled out, his wrinkles had vanished, and his dull eyes had recovered their fire. There, beside the brazier, grinning at my amazement, sat Sherlock Holmes himself. With a slight movement he beckoned me closer. Then, as he half turned towards the room again, he instantly became a doddering old man with slack lips.
“Holmes!” I whispered. “What on earth brings you to this den?”
“Keep your voice as low as possible,” he replied. “My hearing is excellent. If you would kindly dispose of that drunken friend of yours, I should be very glad of a little conversation with you.”
“There is a cab outside.”

“Then please send him home in it. You can safely leave him to himself: he seems too feeble to get into trouble. I suggest you also give the driver a note for your wife, explaining that you have joined forces with me. Wait outside, and I will meet you in five minutes.”

Refusing Sherlock Holmes was difficult. His requests were always so precise, and delivered with such quiet authority. Still, once Whitney was safely inside the cab, my errand would be practically complete. As for what followed, I could wish for nothing better than to join my friend in one of those extraordinary adventures which formed the ordinary pattern of his life. Within a few minutes I had written my note, settled Whitney’s bill, taken him out to the cab, and watched it carry him away into the darkness. Soon afterwards a decrepit figure emerged from the opium den, and I found myself walking down the street beside Sherlock Holmes. For two streets he shuffled along, back bent and steps uncertain. Then he glanced quickly around, drew himself upright, and burst into hearty laughter.
“I imagine, Watson,” he said, “that you suppose I have added opium smoking to my cocaine injections and all the other little weaknesses on which you have kindly offered your medical opinions.”
“It certainly surprised me to find you there.”
“No more than finding you surprised me.”
“I was looking for a friend.”
“I was looking for an enemy.”
“An enemy of yours?”

“Yes, one of my natural enemies—or perhaps I should say my natural prey. In brief, Watson, I am engaged in a most remarkable investigation. I hoped to discover a clue in these drunkards’ incoherent ramblings, as I have done on previous occasions. Had anyone recognised me in that den, my life would not have been safe for an hour. I have used the place for my own purposes before, and the villainous Lascar who runs it has sworn revenge. At the back of the building, near the corner of Paul’s Wharf, there is a trapdoor that could tell some strange stories about what has passed through it on moonless nights.”
“What! Surely you do not mean bodies?”

“Yes, bodies, Watson. A thousand pounds for every poor soul murdered in that den would make us wealthy men. It is the foulest deathtrap along the whole riverside, and I fear Neville St. Clair has entered it never to come out again. But our carriage ought to be here.” He put his two forefingers between his teeth and gave a shrill whistle. A matching whistle answered from a distance, soon followed by rattling wheels and the clatter of horses’ hooves.
“Now, Watson,” said Holmes, as a tall dog-cart came swiftly through the gloom, its side lanterns casting two golden tunnels of light. “You will come with me, won’t you?”
“If I can be any help.”
“A reliable comrade is always helpful, and someone to record the adventure even more so. My room at The Cedars has two beds.”
“At The Cedars?”
“Yes, Mr. St. Clair’s house. I am staying there while I carry out the investigation.”
“And where is that?”
“Near Lee in Kent. There is a seven-mile drive ahead of us.”
“But I know nothing about this.”

“Naturally. You will hear everything shortly. Climb up here. Very good, John; we shall not need you. Here is half a crown. Expect me tomorrow at about eleven. Give the mare her head. Goodbye for now!”

He flicked the horse with his whip, and we sped through a seemingly endless succession of dark, deserted streets. These gradually widened until we were racing across a broad bridge with stone balustrades, the murky river moving sluggishly below. Beyond it stretched another dreary wilderness of brick and mortar. Only a policeman’s heavy, regular tread or the singing and shouting of some late party of revellers disturbed the silence. Dark clouds drifted slowly across the sky, with a star or two shining faintly through their gaps. Holmes drove without speaking, his head bowed upon his chest, apparently deep in thought. Beside him, I wondered what new investigation could be taxing his abilities so severely, but did not dare interrupt his train of thought. We had travelled several miles and were approaching the outer ring of suburban villas when he stirred, shrugged his shoulders, and lit his pipe, like a man who has decided he is taking the best course.

“You have a splendid talent for silence, Watson,” he said. “It makes you an invaluable companion. On my word, I am grateful to have someone to talk to: my own thoughts are far from pleasant. I was wondering what to say tonight when that dear little woman meets me at her door.”
“You forget that I have heard nothing about it.”

“There is just time to explain the facts before we reach Lee. The case seems absurdly simple, yet somehow I cannot find anything to work from. There is plenty of thread, certainly, but I cannot get hold of an end. Let me set it out clearly and briefly, Watson. Perhaps you will catch a glimmer where I see nothing but darkness.”
“Then go ahead.”

“Some years ago—in May 1884, to be precise—a gentleman named Neville St. Clair arrived at Lee. He appeared to have considerable means. He took a large villa, arranged its grounds very attractively, and generally lived in comfort and style. Gradually he made friends locally. In 1887 he married a local brewer’s daughter, and they now have two children. He had no profession, but held interests in several companies. Usually he went into London in the morning and returned each evening on the 5:14 from Cannon Street. Mr. St. Clair is now thirty-seven. His habits are moderate; he is a good husband, an affectionate father, and popular with everyone who knows him. I should add that, as far as we can establish, his present debts total eighty-eight pounds ten shillings, while he has two hundred and twenty pounds in the Capital and Counties Bank. There is therefore no reason to suppose financial worries have been troubling him.

“Last Monday Neville St. Clair went into town a little earlier than usual. Before leaving, he said he had two important errands and would bring his little boy a box of building bricks. By pure chance, shortly after he left that same Monday, his wife received a telegram. A small but valuable parcel she had been expecting was waiting at the Aberdeen Shipping Company’s offices. If you know your London well, you will know those offices are in Fresno Street, off Upper Swandam Lane, where you found me tonight. Mrs. St. Clair had lunch, went into the City, did some shopping, called at the company’s office, and collected her parcel. At exactly 4:35 she found herself walking along Swandam Lane towards the station. Have you followed all that?”
“That is perfectly clear.”

“You may remember how extremely hot Monday was. Mrs. St. Clair walked slowly, looking around for a cab, since she disliked the neighbourhood. As she went along Swandam Lane, she suddenly heard an exclamation or cry. To her horror, she saw her husband looking down from an open second-floor window, apparently beckoning to her. She could see his face quite clearly and described it as terribly agitated. He waved his hands frantically towards her, then disappeared from the window so abruptly that she thought some irresistible force had pulled him back from behind. Her quick feminine eye noticed one peculiar detail: although he had on a dark coat like the one in which he had left for town, he wore neither a collar nor a necktie.

“Certain that something was wrong, she rushed down the steps, for the building was the very opium den where you found me tonight. She ran through the front room and tried to climb the stairs to the first floor. At their foot, however, she encountered the Lascar scoundrel I mentioned. He forced her back and, with help from a Dane employed there as his assistant, pushed her into the street. Distracted by doubts and fears, she hurried down the lane. By exceptional good fortune, in Fresno Street she met an inspector and several constables on their way to their beats. The inspector and two officers went back with her. Despite the proprietor’s continuing resistance, they reached the room where her husband had last appeared. He was nowhere to be seen. Indeed, the entire floor contained nobody except a hideous crippled wretch who apparently lived there. Both he and the Lascar insisted that no one else had occupied the front room that afternoon. Their denials were so emphatic that the inspector hesitated. He had almost decided Mrs. St. Clair had been mistaken when she cried out, sprang towards a small deal box on the table, and tore off its lid. A shower of children’s bricks fell out. They were the toy her husband had promised to bring home.

“That discovery, together with the cripple’s obvious discomposure, convinced the inspector that something serious had happened. The rooms were searched thoroughly, and everything pointed towards a dreadful crime. The front room was a simply furnished sitting-room leading into a small bedroom that faced the rear of one of the wharves. A narrow strip of ground separates the wharf from the bedroom window. At low tide it is dry; at high tide at least four and a half feet of water cover it. The bedroom has a wide window which opens upwards from the bottom. Examination revealed traces of blood on its sill and several scattered drops on the wooden bedroom floor. Hidden behind a curtain in the sitting-room were all Neville St. Clair’s clothes except his coat. His boots, socks, hat, and watch were all there. None of the clothing showed signs of violence, and no other trace of the man could be found. Apparently he must have gone through the window, since there was no other exit. The sinister bloodstains on the sill offered little hope that he could have saved himself by swimming: the tide was at its highest when the tragedy occurred.

“Now for the villains apparently involved. The Lascar was known to have a thoroughly disreputable past. But according to Mrs. St. Clair he was at the foot of the stairs within seconds of her husband’s appearance at the window, so he could hardly have been anything more than an accomplice. He defended himself by professing complete ignorance. He claimed to know nothing of the activities of his lodger, Hugh Boone, and said he could offer no explanation whatever for the missing gentleman’s clothes being there.

“That disposes of the Lascar manager. Now consider the sinister cripple who lives on the opium den’s second floor, certainly the last person to set eyes on Neville St. Clair. His name is Hugh Boone, and anyone who frequents the City knows his hideous face. He begs professionally, though to evade police regulations he pretends to sell a few wax matches. A little way along Threadneedle Street, on the left, you may have noticed a small recess in the wall. There he sits every day, cross-legged, with his tiny stock of matches in his lap. His appearance is so pitiable that a steady sprinkling of charitable coins falls into the greasy leather cap on the pavement beside him. I have watched him more than once, long before I imagined encountering him professionally, and have been astonished by how much he collects in a short time. His looks are so striking that nobody can pass without noticing him: a mass of orange hair, a pale face marred by a terrible scar which draws the outer edge of his upper lip upwards, a bulldog chin, and piercing dark eyes that contrast oddly with his hair. All these distinguish him from ordinary beggars. So does his wit: he always has an answer ready for the jokes passers-by make at his expense. This, then, is the man we now discover lodging at the opium den, the last man to see the gentleman we are seeking.”
“But he is a cripple!” I said. “What could he have done alone against a man in the prime of life?”
